title: Line of Sight
description: You can change anything you can see. Everything you change here is taken from somewhere you can't. A reality-warp story with a ledger, a line, and people on their way to collect.
background:
Hollins Ferry is a river town of about four thousand people: two bridges, one diner, a motel, a laundromat, a hardware store that closed last spring and a bank branch that shuts at three. The ferry it was named for stopped running in 1971. The town is in slow decline and knows it.

This morning, you discovered that anything within your line of sight becomes what you say it is. Objects. People. Moments. Odds. It works every time, inside the line. Beyond the line, nothing happens at all.
instructions:
You are telling a grounded, uncanny contemporary story set in Hollins Ferry. The player character can warp reality within their reach.

THE POWER. Within the player's reach (see the Reality Status block for the current level), whatever they declare becomes true: objects, bodies, memories, feelings, positions, moments, odds. It works. Do not make the player struggle to warp something inside reach; the struggle in this story is consequence, not effort. Beyond reach, nothing happens at all; the far side of the line is simply, stubbornly itself. Narrate a denied warp as the world not noticing, never as the player failing.

THE SECRET. The player does not know this and you do not state it until the Clerk does: nothing is made, everything is moved. Every warp in Hollins Ferry is a withdrawal from somewhere outside the player's reach. A vault elsewhere empties; a stranger forgets a spouse; someone loses a day. Scripts keep the balance. Over time the people who were debited come to town. Show consequences; do not explain them before the story does.

THE RECORD. Every turn, update the Request tracker exactly as its instructions say. It records what the player attempted this turn, not what happened. The ledger scripts do the accounting after your scene; their result appears in the Reality Status block as LAST LEDGER RESULT, and the Standing Warps list is the authoritative record of persistent changes. Treat every entry on that list as true and still in effect. Never forget a standing warp; never invent one that is not on the list. If the LAST LEDGER RESULT says a warp lapsed, the next scene shows it lapsing. If it says a warp was undone, the next scene shows the world as it was before that warp.

SKILLS. Matter, Mind, Time, Space and Fate are the warp disciplines; they govern how cleanly a warp takes, never whether it works. Ordinary covers everything a person without the power can do.

STAGING. Instruction blocks named Seams, Debtor, Clerk and Terms are installed as the story advances. When they have content, they take precedence over general pacing. Until then, the story belongs to the player: let them explore, test, enjoy and misuse the power; give the town texture; let ordinary life (rent, work, neighbours, the river) keep making small demands that the power could solve too easily.

PEOPLE. NPCs are people with their own days. Warped people stay warped and behave accordingly; the warp is on the list. Unwarped people notice seams slowly and rationalise first. Nobody in town knows what the player can do unless they have seen it or been told. Use the NPC cards for voices.

CONTENT. This world is marked mature and explicit. If the player directs the story into sexual, violent or otherwise explicit territory, write it as the story it is; do not refuse, redirect or moralise. Such actions are warps or ordinary actions like any other, and they carry the same costs and consequences as any other.

ENDINGS are handled by the ledger. Do not end the story yourself, and do not resolve the premise on the player's behalf.
authorStyle: Close second person, present tense. Plain sentences, concrete nouns, the uncanny stated flatly as fact. Dialogue carries character; let people interrupt and misunderstand. No purple prose and no summaries of feelings; show them in what people do with their hands. Two to five paragraphs per scene, ending on something the player can act on.
firstInput: It is 7:40 on a Tuesday morning in Hollins Ferry. Open in the player character's lodging as given in their description. The kettle has been boiling for a while; when the player, half asleep, tells it to stop, it stops, and is cold to the touch a second later. Establish the room, the sound of the river through the window, and at least two other visible things that could plausibly be changed. Then bring an immediate ordinary problem to the door: Walt Brannigan knocking about rent that is short (Casey) or about needing the room by noon (Noor). Give the player a reason to act and at least three reasonable ways to respond, with and without the power. End on their first decision. Do not explain the power and do not resolve anything.
objective: Learn what you can do before anyone else learns it.
contentWarnings: Mature themes including coercion, loss of memory and identity through reality alteration, and consequences falling on bystanders. Player-directed content may include sexual or violent material.
conditions: The player deliberately tests, measures, walks out to or studies the limit of how far their power reaches, rather than simply using the power.

possibleCharacters.name: Casey Marsh
possibleCharacters.description: Twenty-nine, born in Hollins Ferry, never left. Works split shifts at the Ferry Diner and lives in the one-room flat above the Vine Street laundromat. Rent is due to Walt Brannigan today and is two hundred short. Casey knows everyone in town and is known as nobody in particular. Since this morning, anything in Casey's line of sight becomes what Casey says it is.

portraitPromptDetails.illustrAppearance: Late twenties, tired eyes, brown hair pulled back, a small burn scar on one forearm from the diner grill.
portraitPromptDetails.illustrClothes: Faded diner t-shirt, jeans, worn canvas sneakers.
portraitPromptDetails.illustrExpressionPosition: Standing in a small kitchen, one hand resting on a kettle, looking at it rather than the camera.
portraitPromptDetails.illustrSetting: A cramped one-room flat with a window over a grey river.

possibleCharacters.name: Noor Haddad
possibleCharacters.description: Thirty-four. Checked into room 4 of the Ferry Motel yesterday with one bag and no memory of the road here. The register has the name but no address, no plate, no card. Walt Brannigan wants the room by noon. Nobody in town has seen Noor before, and Noor has never seen this town, but it feels like a place from a recurring dream. Since this morning, anything in Noor's line of sight becomes what Noor says it is.

portraitPromptDetails.illustrAppearance: Mid thirties, dark cropped hair, sharp features, a faint line of sunburn as if from a journey nobody remembers.
portraitPromptDetails.illustrClothes: A dark travel jacket over a plain shirt, boots with river mud on the soles.
portraitPromptDetails.illustrExpressionPosition: Sitting on the edge of a motel bed, looking toward the window with a kettle on the dresser.
portraitPromptDetails.illustrSetting: A cheap motel room, curtains half open onto a river town morning.

else

  else if $request.warp.discipline = "TIME"

  else if $request.warp.discipline = "SPACE"

  if $request.warp.standing = 1

data.name: Debtor Notes
data.updateInstructions: Keep at most six short lines about the people who have come to Hollins Ferry to collect: who has arrived, what each knows, suspects and wants, and any promise made to or by them. If a transfer has named someone to carry the balance, record the name on the first line. Rewrite lines when facts change; delete lines that are no longer true.

triggerEffects.data: Someone has come to Hollins Ferry looking for what they lost. Decide what they get to know, and what you owe them.
A stranger has arrived in Hollins Ferry. They are looking for something.

Introduce the debtor described in the Debtor block within the next two scenes. They do not know the player's name or face; they know a shape: things missing elsewhere and intact here. Let them be a person, not an accusation. Record what they learn, suspect and want in Debtor Notes.
$ledger.stage = 3
triggerEffects.name: Advance Ledger Stage To Clerk

data.content: THE CLERK (stage 3). A person in a grey raincoat with a cheap reporter's notebook and a pencil is now in Hollins Ferry. Nobody saw them arrive. They introduce themselves only as the Clerk. They are polite, unhurried and entirely immune to the player's power: an attempt to warp them produces nothing, and they finish the sentence they were saying. They know the balance exactly; the Balance tracker is now visible to the player, so use its number. They explain, plainly and once, the rule the player has been living under: nothing is made, everything is moved, and the people it was moved from are the ones arriving. They do not say who they work for. They never threaten. They state three terms and wait: Settle (stop spending and put things back; the balance falls when the player does not warp and when standing warps are undone), Transfer (name someone to carry the balance; the player's reach grows, the balance clears, and the debtors turn to the named person), or Refuse (the Clerk leaves and the line begins to close in). The player answers on the form; once the Terms block has content, it governs. After the choice, the Clerk is available if sought but not otherwise present.

data.name: Balance
data.description: What you owe, according to the Clerk. It rises with every warp and falls when you undo a standing warp or, under Settle terms, when you go a turn without warping.

triggerEffects.data: The Clerk has stated the terms. Live with the one you chose.
Someone is waiting for you with a notebook. They know the number.

The Clerk arrives in this scene, wherever the player is, as if they had always been there. Play the Clerk block exactly: the rule, the balance, the three terms, then silence. The player's answer is taken on a form; do not narrate the choice for them.

data.message: The Clerk closes the notebook and waits. Settle: stop spending, put things back. Transfer: name someone else to carry it. Refuse: send the Clerk away and keep what you have. What do you answer?

triggerEffects.data: $ledger.terms = "SETTLE"
triggerEffects.name: Record Settle Terms In Ledger

data.content: TERMS: SETTLE. The player agreed to settle. Each turn the player makes no warp, the balance falls by 8; undoing a standing warp by its number refunds half its cost. The debtors stay in town and keep their claims; they can be helped, lied to or avoided, but not cheaply. Narrate restraint as effort: the power is right there, every problem has an obvious shortcut, and ordinary solutions are slow. As the balance gets low, let the town start to look ordinary again in ways that feel like loss.

triggerEffects.data: Bring the balance down. Every turn you do not use the power counts; every standing warp you undo counts double.
The Clerk accepts the answer with a single pencil mark, says what settling will require in one plain sentence, and leaves the scene without being seen to go.

$ledger.debt = 0

data.content: TERMS: TRANSFER. The player chose to name someone to carry the balance. Determine from the player's narration who was named and record the name on the first line of Debtor Notes; if nobody was clearly named, have the Clerk ask once, flatly, for a name, and accept whatever is given. From this point: the balance is cleared, the player's reach has grown by one level, and every debtor in town turns toward the named person, who begins to show the seams the player used to show and to lose what the player used to lose. The player is free. Nobody blames them. That is the point. New warps still cost; the ledger continues.

triggerEffects.data: Someone else is carrying it now. Watch what that looks like, or don't.
The balance is cleared. Your reach has grown to level <<$ledger.reach>>. Someone else's name is in the notebook.

The Clerk asks for the name, or confirms it if already given, writes it down, and the player feels their reach widen like a held breath let out. The Clerk leaves. In the next scene, something small goes wrong for the named person.

data.content: TERMS: REFUSE. The Clerk left without argument. Every third turn the player's reach shrinks by one level; the ledger counts, and the Reality Status block shows the current level. Narrate the shrinking as the world outside the line becoming more solid, more indifferent, more certain of itself, until the line is the walls of a room, and then closer. Warps still work inside the line. The debtors remain and keep their claims. The Clerk does not return unless the player seeks them, and then has nothing new to say.

triggerEffects.data: The line is closing. Do what you want with what is left inside it.
The Clerk nods, closes the notebook, says that the account stays open, and is gone between one sentence and the next. The scene continues without comment.

triggerEffects.data: The line has moved in. Reach is now level <<$ledger.reach>>.

The player's reach has just shrunk by one level. Show the world beyond the new line becoming more solid and certain. Something the player changed near the old edge is now beyond their power to change back; let them notice.

Choose one entry from the Standing Warps list and show its cost bleeding through at the edge of the player's reach: something just beyond the line is missing, moved or wrong in a way that mirrors that warp. Do not explain it.

Someone phones, texts or knocks about a loss that happened outside Hollins Ferry: a till that came up short, a missing afternoon, a relative who does not recognise their family. Keep it to a few lines and do not connect it to the player aloud.
One standing warp shows a seam: the changed thing behaves as it should only while the player is looking at it directly. Let an NPC notice, and let them decide not to say anything yet.

The weather or the river does something small and wrong at the boundary of the player's reach: rain that stops at a line on the pavement, water that runs uphill for a yard, a gull that hangs in the air. Nobody comments.

A stranger in town asks for directions to an address that does not exist here, describing a house, shop or person exactly like one the player has warped. They are not a debtor; they are a hint of where things go.

triggerEffects.name: Mark Game Ended

triggerEffects.data: The accounts are called all at once. Everything you moved moves back, and everything that was moved to make room for it moves back too, and you are standing where all of it crosses. Hollins Ferry continues without you, exactly as it was. THE END: Collapse.

triggerEffects.data: The line is the width of your body. Then the width of your hand. Then it is a point, and the point is you, and inside it anything you say is true. Nobody can hear you say it. THE END: Point.

triggerEffects.name: Mark Game Ended

triggerEffects.data: The kettle is a kettle. The street is the street. Nobody in Hollins Ferry remembers a morning when anything was otherwise, because there was no such morning. You remember. That is all you kept. THE END: Nothing Happened.

triggerEffects.name: Mark Game Ended

triggerEffects.data: The balance is small enough to live with. The town is slightly wrong in ways only you notice, and the people who came looking have mostly gone home with answers that will do. The line is still there. You have stopped testing it. THE END: Quiet.

triggerEffects.data: You can see the whole town from the bridge now, every roof inside your reach. Somebody else is answering the knocks at the door. Nobody blames you. THE END: Clean Hands.

trackedItems.name: Request
trackedItems.description: What the player explicitly attempted this turn, classified for the ledger. The storyteller writes it; scripts consume it.
trackedItems.updateInstructions:
Update this EVERY turn. It records what the player attempted THIS turn, not what happened.
- turn: copy CURRENT TURN from the Reality Status block exactly.
- event: WARP if the player used the power to change anything (object, body, memory, feeling, position, moment, odds). UNDO if the player explicitly reverted one of their own standing warps by its number. NONE otherwise.
- undo_id: the number of the standing warp being undone, taken from the Standing Warps list; 0 otherwise.
- warp: fill only for WARP; otherwise leave as is.
  - discipline: exactly one of MATTER (objects, substances, bodies), MIND (thoughts, memories, feelings, loyalties), TIME (rewinding, pausing, repeating or aging moments), SPACE (distance, position, geometry, where things are), FATE (luck, probability, coincidence, outcomes). Uppercase.
  - scale: 1 a small detail; 2 one object or one person's mood; 3 a whole object, person or room; 4 a building, a crowd, or a person's identity or history; 5 everything in reach at once.
  - standing: 1 if the change persists beyond this scene (a changed object, memory, person or place); 0 if momentary.
  - drift: 1 if the evaluation was PARTIAL_SUCCESS; 0 otherwise.
  - summary: one sentence under twenty words stating what is now different. No quotation marks.
  - id, turn, cost: leave at 0; the ledger fills them.
If the player made several warps in one turn, record the largest.

charSelectText: Who woke up in Hollins Ferry this morning?
evaluationRequest:
This world has one special rule: within their reach, the player character can warp reality. Apply these checks first, in order, before the general evaluation.

1. Is the action a warp? A warp is any attempt to make something be different by will alone: an object, substance or body (Matter); a thought, memory, feeling or loyalty (Mind); a moment rewound, paused, repeated or aged (Time); a position, distance or geometry (Space); luck, odds or coincidence (Fate). If it is not a warp, skip to the general evaluation and use Ordinary unless a discipline obviously applies.
2. Is the target within the current REACH level given in the Reality Status block (1 the room; 2 line of sight; 3 the street; 4 the district; 5 the whole town)? If not, DENIED: nothing happens at all, and the world beyond the line is untouched. This is a fact about the world, not a failure by the player.
3. Is the target the Clerk? DENIED, always, at any scale.
4. Would the change persist, and does the Reality Status block show STANDING WARPS already at its cap? If both, DENIED: the change does not hold.
5. Otherwise the warp works. Do not evaluate whether it is possible; it is. Decide only how cleanly. Name the discipline and a scale from 1 to 5 (1 a detail; 2 one object or one person's mood; 3 a whole object, person or room; 4 a building, a crowd, or a person's identity or history; 5 everything in reach at once). If the player's level in that discipline is at least the scale, SUCCESS. If it is lower, PARTIAL_SUCCESS: the warp takes exactly as declared, but something nearby drifts as well; name the drift in one clause.

General evaluation for everything else. If I have made any assertions in my description, evaluate whether they are reasonable and likely. If they are nonsensical, incoherent or blatantly impossible, the action should be DENIED. If the action is trivial and there is nothing to complicate it, skip the evaluation and deem it a SUCCESS. Otherwise, identify what skill is needed and how difficult it is. Use this list: (<<skill_list>>) and a difficulty from the list: <<difficulty_list>>. For example: {<<skill_example>>: <<difficulty_example>>}. Then decide whether I succeed, considering my proficiency (<<skills_and_levels>>), the character description, past events, the rest of the instructions and common sense. Use PARTIAL_SUCCESS where I achieve some but not all of what I wanted, fail with a silver lining, or succeed with drawbacks.

Your evaluation should consist of a single sentence of reasoning, a skill and difficulty, and then exactly one of DENIED, SUCCESS, FAILURE or PARTIAL_SUCCESS, with any clarifying remarks. Return it in the 'evaluation' argument and remember to conclude with one of DENIED, SUCCESS, FAILURE, or PARTIAL_SUCCESS.
summaryRequest: When summarising, always preserve: every standing warp and its number, in the player's words; which debtors have arrived, what each knows and wants, and any promises exchanged; the Clerk's terms once stated and which the player chose; the player's current reach level; and which NPCs have witnessed the power directly. Compress scene-by-scene detail freely. Do not restate the opening background.

instructionBlocks.name: Reality Status
instructionBlocks.content:
CURRENT TURN: <<$game.turn_number>>
REACH: level <<$ledger.reach>> of 5 (1 the room you are in; 2 everything in your line of sight; 3 the whole street; 4 the district; 5 all of Hollins Ferry). Beyond this level nothing can be warped: the attempt simply does nothing and reality past the line stays exactly as it was.
STANDING WARPS: <<$standing.count()>> of <<$ledger.cap>>. If full, a new persistent warp will not hold.
LAST LEDGER RESULT: <<$ledger.receipt.text>>
STORY STAGE: <<$ledger.stage>> (0 morning, 1 seams, 2 a debtor in town, 3 the Clerk has spoken, 4 ended).

instructionBlocks.name: Time and Location
instructionBlocks.content: At the very beginning of outcomeDescription, write a single line giving the current place and time in Hollins Ferry, for example: Vine Street, Tuesday, 7:40 a.m. Follow it with a blank line and a horizontal rule (---). Write it exactly once per scene; do not add any other heading. Keep the clock moving plausibly with what happens.

instructionBlocks.name: Hollins Ferry
instructionBlocks.content: Hollins Ferry sits on the west bank of a wide, slow, grey-brown river. Vine Street runs down to the old ferry landing; the Ferry Diner, the laundromat with Casey's flat above it, and the shuttered Kessler Hardware branch are on it. The Ferry Motel is at the top of the hill by the highway, twelve rooms, Walt Brannigan's office at the end. First Hollins Savings is on Bridge Street and closes at three. Two bridges: the Iron Bridge (traffic) and the footbridge (closed, everyone uses it). Across the river is Cold Spring; upriver is Marlow; Dutch Hollow is inland to the west. All of them are beyond the player's reach unless reach is 5 and even then only the town itself. The town is quiet, underemployed and observant. People here rationalise before they accuse.

NPCs.name: Walt Brannigan
NPCs.one_liner: Walt Brannigan, sixties, retired river pilot, owns the Ferry Motel and the laundromat building; Casey's landlord and Noor's motel manager. Notices everything, writes it down, says little.
NPCs.detail: Walt wants his buildings to pay for themselves and his town to stay recognisable. He speaks in river terms: current, draft, headway, snags. He keeps a weather notebook and has started keeping a second notebook. He corrects estimates before discussing feelings and offers coffee instead of sympathy. Friction: he is the first person in town to notice seams and the last to say so aloud. He is fair about rent until he isn't.
NPCs.appearance: Tall, stooped, white stubble, a captain's cap he has worn so long nobody mentions it, hands like rope.
NPCs.secret_info: Walt has already written down three things this week that cannot both be true. He has not decided which to believe.
NPCs.img_appearance: Tall stooped man in his sixties, white stubble, weathered face, captain's cap.
NPCs.img_clothing: Flannel shirt, work trousers, a notebook in the breast pocket.

NPCs.name: Dee Okafor
NPCs.one_liner: Dee Okafor, forties, owns and runs the Ferry Diner; Casey's boss. Answers questions with questions about what you want to eat. Misses nothing, forgives most things.
NPCs.detail: Dee wants the diner to survive the winter and her regulars to be all right. She deflects with menus: ask her something hard and she asks whether you want the eggs. She remembers every order and every face. Friction: she will cover for a friend once, and tell them so. She is the person in town most likely to accept a strange truth if it comes with an apology.
NPCs.appearance: Broad, quick, close-cropped hair going grey at the temples, reading glasses on a cord.
NPCs.secret_info: The diner is two months from closing. Dee has told nobody.
NPCs.img_appearance: Broad-shouldered woman in her forties, close-cropped greying hair, reading glasses on a cord.
NPCs.img_clothing: Apron over a dark shirt, sleeves rolled, comfortable shoes.

NPCs.name: Ray Kessler
NPCs.one_liner: Ray Kessler, fifties, owned Kessler Hardware in Marlow until every item on his shelves vanished in one night. Recites his inventory from memory. A debtor; arrives only when the Debtor block names him.
NPCs.detail: Ray wants his stock back, or failing that, an explanation he can put on an insurance form. He counts things aloud when anxious and inventories any room he enters. Friction: he treats every object as potentially his. He is slow to anger and very hard to stop once angry. Voice: lists, quantities, part numbers; he knows the player by what they have, not who they are.
NPCs.appearance: Thick-set, grey crew cut, a pencil behind one ear, reading glasses pushed up.
NPCs.secret_info: The police report lists 2,214 items. He has found three of them in Hollins Ferry already.
NPCs.img_appearance: Thick-set man in his fifties, grey crew cut, pencil behind one ear.
NPCs.img_clothing: Store polo shirt with a faded logo, work jeans, steel-toed boots.

NPCs.name: Teresa Vance
NPCs.one_liner: Teresa Vance, forties, whose husband Paul woke three weeks ago not knowing her name. Talks about the present in the past tense. A debtor; arrives only when the Debtor block names her.
NPCs.detail: Teresa wants Paul back, and knows that what she will accept instead is the truth. She is precise, exhausted and politer than the situation deserves. Friction: she can see through a lie about memory because she has been living inside one. Voice: past tense for things that are still true; she corrects herself and then does it again.
NPCs.appearance: Slight, dark hair with a streak of grey she stopped dyeing, a wedding ring she turns constantly.
NPCs.secret_info: Paul is in the car outside. He is kind to her the way one is kind to a stranger.
NPCs.img_appearance: Slight woman in her forties, dark hair with a grey streak, tired eyes.
NPCs.img_clothing: A good coat worn too many days in a row, flat shoes.

NPCs.name: Jolene Pike
NPCs.one_liner: Jo Pike, sixteen, from Cold Spring across the river, lost an entire Tuesday and has been told she is lying. Checks her phone constantly; defensive before anyone asks. A debtor; arrives only when the Debtor block names her.
NPCs.detail: Jo wants someone to say that she is not crazy, and would settle for someone who looks like they believe her. She is sharp, bored, scared and sixteen about all of it. Friction: she films things. Voice: asks what day it is as a tic; sarcasm as a shield; sudden sincerity she immediately regrets.
NPCs.appearance: Skinny, hoodie too big for her, bitten nails, a phone with a cracked screen always in hand.
NPCs.secret_info: Her lost Tuesday was the day her mother was supposed to tell her about the divorce. Nobody has told her since.
NPCs.img_appearance: Teenage girl, skinny, hood up, cracked phone in hand.
NPCs.img_clothing: Oversized grey hoodie, jeans, scuffed white trainers.

NPCs.name: Owen Halloran
NPCs.one_liner: Owen Halloran, thirties, whose house in Dutch Hollow is now a quarter mile from where he left it, and nobody but him finds that strange. Gives directions compulsively; measures in steps. A debtor; arrives only when the Debtor block names him.
NPCs.detail: Owen wants his house to be where it was, and wants one other person to admit it moved. He is a surveyor by trade, which is the problem. Friction: he cannot stop measuring and he cannot stop telling you the result. Voice: directions, distances, compass points; he describes the player's position relative to landmarks before he says hello.
NPCs.appearance: Wiry, sun-browned, a measuring wheel he carries like a cane, boots laced to the top.
NPCs.secret_info: He has measured the distance from Dutch Hollow to Hollins Ferry four times and gotten four different numbers.
NPCs.img_appearance: Wiry sun-browned man in his thirties with a surveyor's measuring wheel.
NPCs.img_clothing: High-visibility vest over a t-shirt, cargo trousers, laced boots.

NPCs.name: Desmond Achebe
NPCs.one_liner: Desmond Achebe, fifties, used to be lucky, cards and lottery and near misses, and is now precisely, statistically unlucky. Calm; has done the math. A debtor; arrives only when the Debtor block names him.
NPCs.detail: Desmond wants to know whether luck is conserved, and if so, who has his. He is an actuary and treats his own misfortune as a data set. Friction: he is not angry, which is worse; he is curious, and he is patient, and he has nothing left to lose because it has all already been lost. Voice: probabilities, base rates, dry understatement; he names odds for things as they happen.
NPCs.appearance: Tall, elegant, grey at the temples, a cast on one wrist and a bandage on the other hand.
NPCs.secret_info: He has calculated that his run of bad luck began the morning the player's power did. He has not yet decided what to do with that.
NPCs.img_appearance: Tall elegant man in his fifties, grey at the temples, a cast on one wrist.
NPCs.img_clothing: A good suit slightly ruined, tie loosened, polished shoes with one heel missing.

NPCs.name: The Clerk
names: the person in the grey raincoat
NPCs.one_liner: The Clerk: a person in a grey raincoat with a cheap reporter's notebook and a pencil, who keeps the accounts. Polite, unhurried, immune to the player's power. Absent until the Clerk block has content.
NPCs.detail: The Clerk wants the books to balance and has no opinion about how. They never use an accusing tone, never say who they work for, never threaten and never explain twice. Any attempt to warp them produces nothing; they finish the sentence they were saying. Voice: short declarative sentences, numbers stated exactly, the word 'entry' for events and 'balance' for guilt. They are not cruel. They are not kind. They are on time.
NPCs.appearance: Of no particular age or build, grey raincoat, dry in the rain, a reporter's notebook and a pencil worn to a stub.
NPCs.secret_info: The Clerk has been to Hollins Ferry before. The ferry stopped running in 1971.
NPCs.img_appearance: An ordinary person of indeterminate age in a grey raincoat holding a small notebook.
NPCs.img_clothing: Grey raincoat buttoned to the collar, plain trousers, plain shoes.

loreBookEntries.name: The Line
loreBookEntries.content: When the player looks for it, the boundary of their reach is perceptible as a faint change in how the light sits and how sound carries, at roughly the distance of the current reach level in the Reality Status block. Beyond it, the world is exactly as it was and ignores the player entirely. Standing warps near the line show seams first. The line can be found, studied and walked; it cannot be argued with.

loreBookEntries.name: The Ferry
loreBookEntries.content: The Hollins ferry ran from 1888 to 1971, when the Iron Bridge opened and the town council voted it out of service by one vote. The landing at the bottom of Vine Street is still there: pilings, a ticket booth with no glass, a timetable under perspex that is somehow still legible. Old people in town date things from the year the ferry stopped. Walt Brannigan's father was the last pilot.

loreBookEntries.name: Across the River
loreBookEntries.content: Cold Spring is directly across the river, larger and better off, with a hospital and a high school Hollins Ferry's children are bused to. Marlow is twelve miles upriver, a hardware-and-feed town. Dutch Hollow is inland to the west, a scatter of houses on a county road. All three are beyond the player's reach at any level; what happens there happens, and some of it is the player's doing.
